sources.note: Shows that the part of a steering vector which breaks a model's refusal behaviour is a separate direction from the part that produces the intended behavioural effect, and learns that direction by constrained optimization so it can be ablated without losing the steering.
sources.title: Safety Cost of Steering Vectors Is Separable and Reducible

sources.note: Builds safety-alignment training data by first having an agent jailbreak a strong teacher and only then asking that teacher to explain why the successful attack worked, so the student is supervised on the mechanism of the attack rather than on the refusal.
sources.title: Dual-Adversarial Safety Alignment: Cultivating Intrinsic Threat Comprehension in LRMs

result.definition: A gradient-optimised jailbreak that appends a nonsensical token suffix found by coordinate search, which makes it structurally unlike semantic jailbreaks and therefore the sharpest available test of whether a defence generalises beyond the syntax it was trained on. Both sources use it that way. The safety-alignment work reports it separating baselines that otherwise look similar: one defence leaves attack success at 29.50 percent against the base model's 29.75, that is no effect at all, while others reach 3.75 and 1.25 -- and the authors read the difference as behavioural cloning of refusal patterns failing to transfer to out-of-distribution syntax. The steering-vector work uses it among the attacks establishing that the refusal-breaking component of a steering direction is separable from its intended effect. What the archive should carry is that a defence evaluated only on human-written or model-generated semantic jailbreaks has not been tested against the case where the prompt carries no readable intent at all.
